common_name: White Fusion Calathea (Pink-and-White Variegated Prayer Plant)

planting.note: Move outdoors to a shaded location after temperatures remain reliably above 55°F; in zone 9 place outdoors April-October and overwinter indoors. White Fusion is one of the most temperamental calatheas, needing consistently high humidity and filtered or rainwater to avoid brown leaf edges.

directions: Plant in deep shade to bright indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist, slightly acidic soil. White Fusion is prized for its irregular, hand-painted-looking foliage pattern of dark green splashed and streaked with creamy white, edged in a fine purple margin, over a deep purple leaf underside — one of the most striking variegation patterns of any commonly grown calathea. It is also one of the more demanding calatheas to keep looking its best, wanting consistently high humidity, evenly moist but never soggy soil, and filtered or rain water rather than tap water, since fluoride and chlorine sensitivity shows up quickly as brown, crispy leaf edges on the white portions. Like other prayer plants it performs a daily nyctinastic leaf movement, folding upward at night and relaxing flat during the day. In zone 9 it thrives as a shaded porch container plant in summer but must move indoors well before temperatures drop into the 50s.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Calathea and Goeppertia Species for Florida

planting.note: Move outdoors to a shaded location after temperatures remain reliably above 55°F; in zone 9 place outdoors April-October and overwinter indoors.

directions: Plant in deep shade to bright indirect light — no direct sun — in well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist, slightly acidic soil. Freddie produces slender, lance-shaped leaves finely pinstriped in alternating light and dark green bands running out from the midrib, a more delicate, feathery pattern than the bold blotched calatheas, with a plain pale green to purple-tinged underside. Its narrower leaves and more upright, clumping habit give it a lighter, grassier texture that works well massed with bolder-leaved shade tropicals for contrast. Maintain consistently moist soil and high humidity, and use filtered or rain water when possible, since brown leaf tips are usually a sign of low humidity or tap-water mineral sensitivity. In zone 9 it performs well as a shaded summer patio plant, moved indoors before temperatures drop into the 50s.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Calathea and Goeppertia Species for Florida

planting.note: Move outdoors to a shaded location after temperatures remain reliably above 55°F; in zone 9 place outdoors April-October and overwinter indoors.

directions: Plant in deep shade to bright indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist, slightly acidic soil. Network is named for its extraordinary leaf pattern of fine, closely spaced light and dark green lines that intersect in a tight mosaic or checkerboard-like grid across the entire leaf surface, a finer and more geometric pattern than the bolder blotched markings of most other calatheas. The dense, even patterning reads almost like a printed fabric and provides strong textural interest even in a mixed planting of other patterned foliage. As with other prayer plants, leaves fold upward at night and flatten during the day, and the plant wants consistently moist, humid conditions with filtered or rain water to avoid the brown leaf-edge scorch that tap-water minerals and low humidity commonly cause. In zone 9 it grows well as a shaded porch or patio container plant through the warm season, moving indoors before temperatures fall into the 50s.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Calathea and Goeppertia Species for Florida

planting.note: Move outdoors to a shaded location after temperatures remain reliably above 55°F; in zone 9 place outdoors April-October and overwinter indoors. Red Valentine tolerates lower light than most other red aglaonema cultivars.

directions: Plant in low to bright indirect light — no direct sun — in well-drained, humus-rich, evenly moist potting mix. Red Valentine produces broad, glossy leaves in shades of deep pink and red overlaid with dark green, irregular markings, giving strong, saturated color that holds up in lower light better than most other colorful houseplants, which is a large part of the aglaonema group's popularity for offices and dim interiors. It is an easygoing, slow-growing plant that tolerates missed waterings and average indoor humidity far better than most tropical foliage plants, forming a dense, clumping rosette over time. Let the potting mix dry slightly between waterings, avoid cold drafts and temperatures below 55°F, and in zone 9 it can spend the warm season on a shaded porch before returning indoors well ahead of frost.

planting.note: Divide rooted offsets from the base and pot in fast-draining succulent or cactus mix; grow outdoors in shade to partial sun in zone 10-11 or as a slow-growing, drought-tolerant indoor houseplant.

directions: Pot in a fast-draining cactus mix and set in bright indirect light to partial sun. Fernwood is a cylindrical-leaved Sansevieria selection whose rounded, channeled leaves fan out and fuse at the base in flattened, overlapping sprays rather than growing as separate spears, giving each rosette an architectural, almost sculptural fan shape distinct from the paddle-leaved snake plants most people know. It is exceptionally drought-tolerant and slow-growing, thriving on neglect and needing water only once the potting mix has dried out completely, and it largely shrugs off the low humidity and inconsistent light of typical indoor spaces. Offsets form slowly at the base and can be divided to start new plants once a clump is well established. Avoid overwatering above all else, since soggy soil is by far the most common cause of rot in any sansevieria.

common_name: Krimson Princess Hoya (White-Centered Variegated Wax Plant)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; Krimson Princess colors most vividly in bright light and blooms most reliably when slightly pot-bound.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix. Krimson Princess is the reverse-variegated sister cultivar to Krimson Queen, with the pattern flipped so a creamy white to pale pink center runs down the middle of each thick, waxy leaf while the margins stay solid green, new growth often flushing a deeper pink in bright light. Vigorous, twining vines eventually produce rounded clusters of small, fragrant, star-shaped pink flowers with a deep red center from the same reusable flowering spurs year after year, so those spurs should never be trimmed off. Provide a trellis or hanging basket for support, let the chunky potting mix dry between waterings, and give bright indirect light for the best variegation, since low light causes the plant to green out.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; Publicalyx blooms most reliably when slightly pot-bound and given bright light.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix. Hoya publicalyx is a fast-growing Philippine species with thick, semi-succulent leaves that are dusted with silvery speckles and flush deep purple-bronze along the margins in bright light, growing on vigorous twining vines that climb or trail readily. Established plants produce large, rounded clusters of dark maroon-purple, star-shaped flowers with a contrasting pale center and a notably strong, sweet fragrance, especially in the evening, from the same reusable flowering spurs each year. It grows and blooms faster than many other hoya species, rewarding a bright window or covered porch with steady growth. Provide a trellis or hanging basket for support, let the potting mix dry between waterings, and never remove the woody flowering spurs.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained potting mix in bright indirect light to partial sun; Nanouk shows its brightest pink coloring with some direct morning sun but scorches in hot afternoon exposure.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in bright indirect light to partial sun, giving some gentle morning sun for the best pink color. Nanouk is a patented tradescantia cultivar with thick, fleshy leaves striped in shades of pink, cream, purple, and green, a bolder and more saturated color combination than the plainer green-and-white or green-and-purple wandering jews it descends from, and the pink intensifies with brighter light. Its dense, mounding, semi-trailing habit works well in a hanging basket, mixed container, or groundcover-style planting, and it roots readily from stem cuttings set in water or moist soil, making it easy to propagate and share. Water when the top inch of soil dries out, and in zone 9a it can grow outdoors as a warm-season groundcover or container plant but should come inside or be treated as an annual before hard frost.
